Relations among exponential integrals, Bessel and Kummer functions

Ruiyi Zhang Independent Researcher, Columbia, Maryland, USA
(Date: November 17, 2026)
Abstract.

We determine algebraic relations among finite families of special functions. The families contain rational-exponential primitives and iterated entire exponential integrals. They also contain Bessel functions of rational order and Kummer functions. The Kummer functions have nonintegral first parameter and second parameter one. We give the transcendence degree and generators of the relation ideal. Explicit maps for normalized entire functions complement Gorelov’s 2019–2021 classification of second-order equations. We then specialize the relations at nonzero algebraic points. Over explicit base fields, we obtain a lower bound for the transcendence degree of mixed connection values together with Euler’s constant, logarithmic constants and, when required, pi. We also prove a linear independence estimate with explicit constants for all sufficiently large heights. It concerns one, the exponential of one, the reciprocal of that exponential and the entire exponential integral at one. The qualitative results use differential Galois theory and E-function specialization. The estimate uses integer polynomial approximations and derivative selection.

Key words and phrases:
algebraic independence, E-functions, differential Galois theory, exponential integral, Bessel functions, confluent hypergeometric functions
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification:
Primary 11J91; Secondary 12H05, 33C10, 33C15

1. Introduction

The transcendence degree of Siegel’s EE-functions [37] is preserved under specialization at nonzero algebraic ordinary points [36]. Beukers lifts relations [10, Theorems 1.1–1.3] using André’s EE-operators [2, 3].

Parameter coincidences, Wronskians and shared logarithmic companions produce mixed relations. We determine their ideal, retaining normalized additive constants. Nonclosed lists are treated by closure, specialization and elimination below.

1.1. A first example

Take c≠0c\neq 0 and the linked blocks Bess⁡(c,0)\operatorname{Bess}(c,0) and Kum⁡(2⁢c,1/2)\operatorname{Kum}(2c,1/2). They form one linkage class and leave three independent coordinates over T=ℂ⁢(z)⁢(ec⁢z)T=\mathbb{C}(z)(e^{cz}) and four over ℂ⁢(z)\mathbb{C}(z). Supplementary Section S4 gives the maps, determinant, series and connections.

For nonclosed lists, close, normalize, adjoin basis exponentials, saturate, specialize and eliminate auxiliary coordinates, retaining duplicate/constant graphs. The enlarged list of values need not have the same transcendence degree as the original list.

Theorem 4 in Appendix D gives a linear independence estimate for 1,e,e−1,Ein⁡(1)1,e,\allowbreak e^{-1},\operatorname{Ein}(1) with evaluated constants. Our H−60/12H^{-60}/12 estimate is weaker than the classical one and applies for H≥H0H\geq H_{0}. Supplementary Section S3 compares the classical exponent and effectiveness and gives a cruder bound for 1≤H<H01\leq H<H_{0}.

Theorem 5 gives a multi-node, mixed-family bound over ℰ\mathcal{E} and the regular-value base BB. The one-point consequence over the full ℰ\mathcal{E} is known [36, Ch. 7, §1, Theorem 1, pp. 232–233]; Supplementary Section S5 gives the finite-rate reduction and distinguishes Mahler’s announcement from Rivoal’s proof. We claim no novelty for the mixed formulation over BB. Section 7 states the bound and cancellation limitations.

1.3. Relation to earlier work

For primitive and homogeneous antecedents see Supplementary Section S5 and Appendix C [33, 27, 11, 23]. Mahler also proved that π⁢Y0⁢(2)/(2⁢J0⁢(2))−γ\pi Y_{0}(2)/(2J_{0}(2))-\gamma is transcendental [29, Theorem 3 and its consequence, pp. 169–170], a precedent for the Bessel connection row. Fischler–Rivoal give a general relation-ideal algorithm [17, Theorem 4(i)–(ii), pp. 2–3 of the arXiv version]. Supplementary Section S5 compares the regular families, their normalizations and the restricted inhomogeneous results.

Twisted residues, integration and SL2\operatorname{SL}_{2} factors determine the pointwise stabilizer of the coordinate field (Lemma 4.10). Integral quotients and equal dimensions then identify the full ideals.

4.1. Primitives and towers

Lemma 4.1.

The tht_{h} are algebraically independent over F1F_{1}, and LL is transcendental over TT. For q∈Fi×q\in F_{i}^{\times}, i=0,1i=0,1, D⁢q/q∈ℂDq/q\in\mathbb{C} forces q∈ℂ×q\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}.

Proof.

Suppose distinct exponentials satisfy a rational linear relation with the fewest terms. Divide by one term, making its coefficient 11, and differentiate. The resulting relation has fewer terms. Thus all its coefficients vanish. A remaining coefficient would give q′/q=−μ≠0q^{\prime}/q=-\mu\neq 0 for rational qq. This is impossible, since a rational logarithmic derivative tends to zero at infinity. Distinct monomials in the tht_{h} have distinct weights. They are therefore linearly independent over F0F_{0}. This proves algebraic independence of the tht_{h}.

A polynomial relation of least positive degree nn for LL over TT can be continued around zero. Its coefficients return to their original values, while LL changes to L+2⁢π⁢iL+2\pi i. Subtraction gives a relation of degree n−1n-1, with leading coefficient 2⁢π⁢i⁢n2\pi in times the former leading coefficient. This is a contradiction. Thus LL is transcendental over TT, and the tht_{h} remain independent over F1F_{1}.

For p=LN+cN−1⁢LN−1+⋯p=L^{N}+c_{N-1}L^{N-1}+\cdots, D⁢pDp has degree N−1N-1 and coefficient cN−1′+N/z≠0c^{\prime}_{N-1}+N/z\neq 0: a rational derivative has zero residue at zero. Every nonzero factor exponent then contributes an uncancelled pole to D⁢q/qDq/q. If D⁢q/qDq/q is constant, no such factor occurs. Thus q∈F0×q\in F_{0}^{\times}. Its logarithmic derivative tends to zero at infinity. It is therefore zero, and q∈ℂ×q\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}. This also proves the assertion for i=0i=0. ∎

A positive-degree monic irreducible p∈ℂ⁢(z)⁢[L]p\in\mathbb{C}(z)[L] satisfies p∤D⁢p≠0p\nmid Dp\neq 0. No nonunit irreducible p∈Rip\in R_{i}, i=0,1i=0,1, divides D⁢pDp. Consequently y∈Frac⁡Riy\in\operatorname{Frac}R_{i} and D⁢y∈RiDy\in R_{i} imply y∈Riy\in R_{i}.

4.2. Groups and twists

Let ℓ\ell be the lcm of nonresonant 2⁢ν02\nu_{0} denominators (ℓ=1\ell=1 if none), and T′=T⁢(z1/ℓ)T^{\prime}=T(z^{1/\ell}). All constants remain ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Lemma 4.6.

The groups are SL2\operatorname{SL}_{2} for order-zero Bessel, have identity component SL2\operatorname{SL}_{2} for nonresonant Bessel, and are GL2\operatorname{GL}_{2} for nonintegral Kummer.

Proof.

Bessel has algebraic Wronskian. Thus G0⊂SL2G^{0}\subset\operatorname{SL}_{2}. The algebraic gauge zνz^{\nu} and x=i⁢c⁢zx=icz reduce to (F6), which excludes a nonzero Liouvillian solution. If G0G^{0} were solvable, the Liouvillian criterion in (F5) would make the Picard–Vessiot (PV) field Liouvillian [38, Theorem 1.43, pp. 33–34]. Every solution would then be Liouvillian. Thus G0G^{0} is not solvable. By (F15), every proper connected subgroup of SL2\operatorname{SL}_{2} is solvable. Thus G0=SL2G^{0}=\operatorname{SL}_{2}. In order zero its Wronskian is rational. Hence G=SL2G=\operatorname{SL}_{2}. For Kummer rescale s=1s=1. A rational invariant line would give

(4.6) r′+r2+(z−1−1)⁢r−a/z=0.r^{\prime}+r^{2}+(z^{-1}-1)r-a/z=0.

Its nonzero finite poles have residue 11. Zero cannot be a pole. At infinity r=ϵ+m/z+O⁢(z−2)r=\epsilon+m/z+O(z^{-2}), ϵ=0\epsilon=0 or 11, with m≥0m\geq 0 the number of finite poles. Substitution gives m=−am=-a or a−1a-1, contrary to a∉ℤa\notin\mathbb{Z}. Thus GG is irreducible. At zero the indicial equation is r2=0r^{2}=0, with resonant exponents (0,0)(0,0). The local solution J=Sa−fa⁢LJ=S_{a}-f_{a}L, with fa⁢(0)=1f_{a}(0)=1, changes to J−2⁢π⁢i⁢faJ-2\pi if_{a} around zero. This gives a nonidentity unipotent in GG. The Zariski closure of its powers is connected by (F15). Thus it lies in G0G^{0}. If G0G^{0} fixed a line, this would be its unique fixed line and normality would make it GG-stable. So G0G^{0} is irreducible. Its unipotent radical is normal [12, §11.21, p. 157]. Its representation image is unipotent [12, §4.5, p. 85] and has a nonzero fixed vector [26, §17.5, Theorem, p. 112]. Normality makes this fixed space G0G^{0}-stable by conjugation. Irreducibility makes it the full solution space, so the faithful radical action is trivial. By (F15), G0⊃SL2G^{0}\supset\operatorname{SL}_{2}. For the original scale ss, the determinant is es⁢z/ze^{sz}/z. Its transcendence makes the determinant character of GG surjective onto 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}. Together with G0⊃SL2G^{0}\supset\operatorname{SL}_{2}, this gives G=GL2G=\operatorname{GL}_{2}. ∎

The formal comparison used below is Lemma A.1, proved in Appendix A.

Lemma 4.7.

A subdirect Lie algebra in 𝔰⁢𝔩2⊕𝔰⁢𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2}\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_{2} is either the full sum or the graph of an inner automorphism.

Proof.

Its intersections with the two factors are ideals in those factors. If either intersection is nonzero, simplicity and surjectivity give the full sum. Otherwise both projections are isomorphisms. Thus the subalgebra is the graph of an automorphism. The elementary proof after (F15) shows that every automorphism of 𝔰⁢𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2} is inner. ∎

Lemma 4.11.

Let AA be a domain and let vv be a unit of AA. The ring Qv=A⁢[X,W,Y,S]/(X⁢W−Y⁢S+v)Q_{v}=A[X,W,Y,S]/(XW-YS+v) is a free AA-module whose basis consists of the monomials not divisible by X⁢WXW. The natural map A⁢[X,Y,S]→QvA[X,Y,S]\to Q_{v} is injective. If AA is a characteristic-zero field, QvQ_{v} is geometrically integral and has dimension three.

Proof.

Use lexicographic order X>Y>S>WX>Y>S>W. The relation is monic with leading monomial X⁢WXW. Division by this monic polynomial gives unique normal forms over AA. Thus the monomials not divisible by X⁢WXW form a free basis. In particular the monomials in X,Y,SX,Y,S remain independent. Over an algebraic closure of a characteristic-zero field, a nontrivial factorization would have two linear factors. Their quadratic part has rank at most two. In contrast, X⁢W−Y⁢SXW-YS has rank four. The polynomial is therefore geometrically irreducible, and its quotient is geometrically integral of dimension three. ∎

Lemma 4.12.

The generators in Theorem 1 generate the full kernels of coordinate evaluation over TT and over 𝒜exp=ℂ⁢(z)⁢[Θ±1]\mathscr{A}_{\exp}=\mathbb{C}(z)[\Theta^{\pm 1}]. Both kernels are prime. The exponential, residue and linkage generators are also graphs. Each eliminates one variable in terms of retained variables. Its coefficient on that variable is 11. Appendix A Foundational facts

An EE-function is an entire series ∑an⁢zn/n!\sum a_{n}z^{n}/n! with algebraic coefficients, h⁢(a0,…,an)=O⁢(n)h(a_{0},\ldots,a_{n})=O(n) and a linear differential equation over ℚ¯⁢[z]{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}[z] [10, p. 369]. Here hh is the absolute logarithmic Weil height of [1:a0:⋯:an][1:a_{0}:\cdots:a_{n}]. Our differential fields have characteristic zero and common algebraically closed constants C0C_{0}.

(F1) For EE-functions f′=A⁢ff^{\prime}=Af, A∈Mn⁢(ℚ¯⁢(z))A\in M_{n}({\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z)), and a common denominator QQ of AA, every algebraic α\alpha with α⁢Q⁢(α)≠0\alpha Q(\alpha)\neq 0 satisfies

trdegℚ¯⁡ℚ¯⁢(f⁢(α))=trdegℚ¯⁢(z)⁡ℚ¯⁢(z)⁢(f)\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}}{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(f(\alpha% ))=\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z)}{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z)% (f)

[10, Theorem 1.1, p. 370].

(F2) Under (F1), each homogeneous relation P⁢(f⁢(α))=0P(f(\alpha))=0 lifts to R∈ℚ¯⁢[z,X]R\in{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}[z,X] homogeneous in XX, with R⁢(z,f)=0R(z,f)=0, R⁢(α,X)=PR(\alpha,X)=P. Adjoin 11 for inhomogeneous relations [10, Theorems 1.2–1.3 and the intervening paragraph, p. 370].

(F3) If primitives with yi′∈Fby_{i}^{\prime}\in F_{\rm b} are algebraically dependent over FbF_{\rm b}, a nonzero constant combination of them belongs to FbF_{\rm b} [33, pp. 315–316]. For the differential-algebraic setting, see [27]; Lemma 4.4 proves the same-constant meromorphic case.

(F4) A subdirect Lie algebra in ⨁𝔰⁢𝔩2\bigoplus\mathfrak{sl}_{2} is a sum of diagonal graphs (Lemma 4.7 and Proposition 4.9). The factor automorphisms are inner, as proved below.

(F5) A fundamental matrix generates a PV extension with trdeg⁡(E/K)=dimGal⁡(E/K)\operatorname{trdeg}(E/K)=\allowbreak\dim\operatorname{Gal}(E/K). Closed subgroups correspond to intermediate fields, normal subgroups to PV subextensions, and invariant subspaces for the full group to differential submodules. Our lower-unitriangular matrices satisfy σ⁢(F)=F⁢Cσ\sigma(F)=FC_{\sigma}, so Cσ=F−1⁢σ⁢(F)C_{\sigma}=F^{-1}\sigma(F) is lower unitriangular. The PV group is algebraic [38, Observation 1.26(2), p. 19; Theorem 1.27(1), p. 20]. Each nonidentity element’s powers have connected additive closure [12, §7.3, Remark, p. 106], proving unipotence and connectedness. Liouvillian PV extensions are exactly those with solvable Galois identity component [38, Theorem 1.43, pp. 33–34].

(F6) The equation x2⁢y′′+x⁢y′+(x2−ν2)⁢y=0x^{2}y^{\prime\prime}+xy^{\prime}+(x^{2}-\nu^{2})y=0 has a nonzero Liouvillian solution exactly for ν∈12+ℤ\nu\in\tfrac{1}{2}+\mathbb{Z} [28, §3.2, Example 2, p. 14; §4.2, Example 2, pp. 19–20]. Nonzero scaling and the algebraic gauges used here preserve this property by direct change of variables.

(F7) The Laurent, logarithmic-derivative and polynomial-log reductions used here are proved in Lemmas 4.2, 4.1 and 4.3.

(F8) Lemma 4.4 proves the all-finite-pole criterion for q=r′+μ⁢rq=r^{\prime}+\mu r.

(F9) Lemma A.1 formally diagonalizes systems with distinct leading eigenvalues and proves invariance of powers modulo ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

(F10) For a2⁢y′′+a1⁢y′+a0⁢y=0a_{2}y^{\prime\prime}+a_{1}y^{\prime}+a_{0}y=0, differentiating the Wronskian gives W′=−(a1/a2)⁢WW^{\prime}=-(a_{1}/a_{2})W.

(F11) Sums, products, derivatives, algebraic rescalings and primitives vanishing at zero preserve EE-functions. The exponential, rational-parameter Kummer and F10{}_{0}F_{1} instances satisfy the exact bounds and equations in Theorem 3’s proof.

(F12) We use DLMF 10.29.1(a), 10.29.3(a)–(b), 10.39.5, 10.40.1, 13.2.9, 13.2.39, 13.2.41, 13.3.17, 13.6.10 and 13.7.2–13.7.3 with their stated branches and sectors. Our equations also imply the linkage maps.

(F13) Tensor products of geometrically integral algebras over a field are geometrically integral [25, Proposition (4.6.5)(ii), p. 69]. For a finitely generated integral kk-algebra AA, dimA=trdegk⁡A\dim A=\operatorname{trdeg}_{k}A [30, Theorem 5.6, p. 34]. Consequently, for primes P⊂P′P\subset P^{\prime} in a finitely generated kk-algebra, equal quotient dimensions imply P=P′P=P^{\prime}. We also use that free modules over domains are torsion-free and that field extensions are free as modules.

(F14) Hermite normal form, number-field factorization and Gröbner elimination are effective over the specified fields [14, §§2.4,3.6], [4]. Appendix B refers to Supplementary Section S2 for model (M-gen). Its oracle (O1) gives integer-relation ℤ\mathbb{Z}-bases for finite tuples.

(F15) Algebraic-group morphisms have closed image; G0G^{0} is normal of finite index. Surjections preserve identity components [12, Proposition 1.2(b), p. 46; Corollary 1.4(a)–(b), p. 47]. In characteristic zero, dimG=dimLie⁡G\dim G=\dim\operatorname{Lie}G. This uses the smooth reduced-group convention of [26, §9.1, p. 65] together with the dimension statement in [12, Proposition 1.2(a), p. 46]. Also Lie⁡ker⁡ϕ=ker⁡d⁢ϕ\operatorname{Lie}\ker\phi=\ker d\phi and Lie⁡(H∩K)=Lie⁡H∩Lie⁡K\operatorname{Lie}(H\cap K)=\operatorname{Lie}H\cap\operatorname{Lie}K [26, §12.5, p. 85]; Lie⁡(ϕ⁢G)=d⁢ϕ⁢(Lie⁡G)\operatorname{Lie}(\phi G)=d\phi(\operatorname{Lie}G) uses [12, §7.2, proof, p. 105]. For connected HH, H⊂KH\subset K iff Lie⁡H⊂Lie⁡K\operatorname{Lie}H\subset\operatorname{Lie}K [26, §13.1, Theorem, p. 87] [12, §7.1(2), p. 105]. For closed H⊂GH\subset G, connected GG and dimH=dimG\dim H=\dim G imply H=GH=G. Apply proper-closed-subset dimension drop to H0H^{0} in irreducible GG [26, §3.2, Proposition, p. 25] [12, Proposition 1.2 and following paragraph, pp. 46–47]. Proper connected SL2\operatorname{SL}_{2} subgroups are solvable by [38, Theorem 4.29, pp. 133–134]. In characteristic zero, nonidentity unipotent powers are dense in a connected additive subgroup [12, §2.1, p. 56; §7.3, Remark, p. 106].

For (F4), work over the algebraically closed characteristic-zero field ℂ\mathbb{C}. Put h=diag⁡(1,−1)h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1), e=E12e=E_{12} and f=E21f=E_{21}. For a Lie automorphism φ\varphi, ad⁡φ⁢(h)\operatorname{ad}\varphi(h) has eigenvalues 0,2,−20,2,-2. A traceless 2×22\times 2 matrix with eigenvalues λ,−λ\lambda,-\lambda has adjoint eigenvalues 0,2⁢λ,−2⁢λ0,2\lambda,-2\lambda. A nilpotent matrix has nilpotent adjoint. Thus φ⁢(h)\varphi(h) has eigenvalues 1,−11,-1. Inner conjugation makes φ⁢(h)=h\varphi(h)=h. The weight spaces give φ⁢(e)=a⁢e\varphi(e)=ae, φ⁢(f)=b⁢f\varphi(f)=bf. Brackets give a⁢b=1ab=1. Choosing t∈ℂ×t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times} with t2=at^{2}=a identifies the remaining automorphism as conjugation by diag⁡(t,t−1)\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1}).

For (F15), let G⊆GL2⁡(ℂ)G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) be a connected reductive algebraic subgroup in its defining representation, and put H=G∩SL2H=G\cap\operatorname{SL}_{2}. If H0H^{0} is proper, it lies in a Borel subgroup or torus and is solvable. The connected commutator [G,G][G,G] lies in H0H^{0}. Since G/HG/H is abelian, Corollary A.38 makes GG solvable. Lie–Kolchin and complete reducibility give an invariant line and complement. Thus GG is conjugate to a connected diagonal subgroup, hence a torus. A non-torus GG therefore contains SL2\operatorname{SL}_{2}. The solvability and invariant-line inputs are [39, Corollary A.38, p. 364; Theorem A.46, p. 367]. Complete reducibility is stated in the unnumbered paragraph after Definition 2.37, p. 59, of the July 2002 draft [38].

Appendix B The input model and computation

Supplementary Section S2 gives the full input model, computability proposition and proof. It requires exact presented fields and compatible normalization constants. Approximations alone are excluded. Appendix A.2 supplies the value coefficient bounds.

Appendix E Detailed proofs of the Galois-group and specialization steps

E.1. The full joint group

We expand the group argument in Proposition 4.9. All groups are reduced complex linear algebraic groups.

Lemma E.1.

Let ϕ:G→H\phi:G\to H be a group morphism. Its image is closed, G0G^{0} is normal of finite index, and

(E.1) ϕ⁢(G0)=ϕ⁢(G)0,dimG=dimLie⁡G,Lie⁡(ker⁡ϕ)=ker⁡d⁢ϕ,Lie⁡(ϕ⁢(G))=d⁢ϕ⁢(Lie⁡G),Lie⁡(A∩B)=Lie⁡A∩Lie⁡B(A,B⊂G⁢ closed).\begin{gathered}\phi(G^{0})=\phi(G)^{0},\qquad\dim G=\dim\operatorname{Lie}G,% \\ \operatorname{Lie}(\ker\phi)=\ker d\phi,\qquad\operatorname{Lie}(\phi(G))=d% \phi(\operatorname{Lie}G),\\ \operatorname{Lie}(A\cap B)=\operatorname{Lie}A\cap\operatorname{Lie}B\quad(A,% B\subset G\text{ closed}).\end{gathered}

If AA is connected, then Lie⁡A⊂Lie⁡B\operatorname{Lie}A\subset\operatorname{Lie}B implies A⊂BA\subset B. A closed subgroup of a connected group with equal dimension is the whole group.

Proof.

Closed images and identity components follow from [12, Proposition 1.2(b), p. 46; Corollary 1.4(a)–(b), p. 47]. Smoothness identifies group dimension with tangent-space dimension [12, Proposition 1.2(a), p. 46] [26, §9.1, p. 65]. The kernel and intersection identities are [26, §12.5, Theorem, p. 85]. The image identity uses characteristic-zero separability [12, §7.2, proof, p. 105]. If Lie⁡A⊂Lie⁡B\operatorname{Lie}A\subset\operatorname{Lie}B, then A∩BA\cap B has dimension dimA\dim A. Connected algebraic groups are irreducible [12, Proposition 1.2 and following paragraph, pp. 46–47]. Proper closed irreducible subsets have smaller dimension [26, §3.2, Proposition, p. 25]. Apply this to (A∩B)0⊂A(A\cap B)^{0}\subset A. It gives A⊂BA\subset B; see also [12, §7.1(2), p. 105] [26, §13.1, Theorem, p. 87]. The last assertion follows by applying the same argument to B0⊂GB^{0}\subset G. ∎

Lemma E.2.

Let E/KE/K and F/KF/K be PV extensions with algebraically closed constants ℂ\mathbb{C}. Assume their compositum M=E⁢FM=EF has the same constants. Then M/KM/K and M/FM/F are PV, and restriction gives

(E.2) Gal⁡(M/F)≃Gal⁡(E/(E∩F)).\operatorname{Gal}(M/F)\simeq\operatorname{Gal}(E/(E\cap F)).

The right side is normal in Gal⁡(E/K)\operatorname{Gal}(E/K). Its quotient is a quotient of Gal⁡(F/K)\operatorname{Gal}(F/K). The intersection E∩FE\cap F is PV over KK. The maps Gal⁡(M/K)→Gal⁡(E/K),Gal⁡(F/K)\operatorname{Gal}(M/K)\to\operatorname{Gal}(E/K),\operatorname{Gal}(F/K) are onto.

Proof.

The block sum of fundamental matrices generates M/KM/K. The matrix for EE also generates M/FM/F. Both subfields E,FE,F are invariant under Gal⁡(M/K)\operatorname{Gal}(M/K). PV Galois correspondence gives the two surjections [38, Proposition 1.34(1)–(2), p. 26]. The restriction Gal⁡(M/F)→Gal⁡(E/K)\operatorname{Gal}(M/F)\to\operatorname{Gal}(E/K) is injective: an automorphism in its kernel fixes EE and FF, hence fixes M=E⁢FM=EF, so it is the identity. Put H=im⁡(Gal⁡(M/F)→Gal⁡(E/K))H=\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{Gal}(M/F)\to\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)). It is closed by Lemma E.1. Surjectivity and conjugation show that HH is normal. Its fixed field is E∩FE\cap F, proving (E.2) by the same correspondence. Since HH is normal, the PV correspondence also makes E∩FE\cap F PV over KK [38, Proposition 1.34(2), p. 26]. The map to Gal⁡(E/K)/H\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)/H kills Gal⁡(M/F)\operatorname{Gal}(M/F). It therefore factors through Gal⁡(F/K)\operatorname{Gal}(F/K). ∎

S2.1. Exact input definition and computation

Definition S2.1.

A presented field k0⊂ℂk_{0}\subset\mathbb{C} has finite representations for its elements. Arithmetic and equality are computable. Its embedding is specified. Model (M-alg) supplies a number field ℚ⁢(θ)\mathbb{Q}(\theta). A minimal polynomial and isolating disc specify θ\theta. In model (M-gen), oracle (O1) takes any finite input tuple. It returns a ℤ\mathbb{Z}-basis of its integer relations. For number fields this oracle is supplied by integer linear algebra. To test a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z}, ask whether there is a relation m⁢a+n=0ma+n=0 with m≠0m\neq 0 and m∣nm\mid n.

The rates, nodes, scales and Kummer parameters belong to k0k_{0}. Bessel orders are supplied as reduced rationals. Rational kernels are supplied as polynomial pairs. Model (M-gen) also supplies their linear denominator factors. In (M-alg), we compute a splitting field. Set k1=k0⁢(poles)k_{1}=k_{0}(\text{poles}). The value statements require (M-alg) and α∈k0×\alpha\in k_{0}^{\times}. The supplied constants γF\gamma_{F} encode the chosen base-point normalization. Thus z∗z_{*} does not enter the computation. A base-point primitive is specified by γF∈k0\gamma_{F}\in k_{0}:

(S2.1) F=∑σ=(μ,p)eμ⁢pres(F)σΦσ+rF+γF.F=\sum_{\sigma=(\mu,p)}e^{\mu p}\operatorname{res}(F)_{\sigma}\Phi_{\sigma}+r_% {F}+\gamma_{F}.

Coordinates of type (B2E) and towers instead use origin normalization. Let 𝒱res,0\mathcal{V}_{{\rm res},0} be the origin-normalized first-level residue span. Write 𝒱res,∗\mathcal{V}_{{\rm res},*} for the base-point-normalized first-level residue span. The list is normalization-compatible when

(S2.2) 𝒱res,0∩𝒱res,∗=0,\mathcal{V}_{{\rm res},0}\cap\mathcal{V}_{{\rm res},*}=0,

or after moving a specified origin subset to the base-point side using supplied γG∈k0\gamma_{G}\in k_{0} satisfying (S2.1). A supplied comparison is assumed correct; its constant is exact input. The algorithm does not evaluate the analytic primitive at the base point. Choose residue bases separately on the two normalization sides. Each fundamental coordinate-basis relation uses one normalization. An arbitrary relation decomposes into the two types. Compatibility holds if all coordinates except possibly LL are origin-normalized. Their residue vectors have ∑μv(μ,0)=0\sum_{\mu}v_{(\mu,0)}=0. For LL, res⁡(L)=e(0,0)\operatorname{res}(L)=e_{(0,0)}. Proposition S2.2.

In both input models, the quantities d,ρ,τ,#⁢𝒞d,\rho,\tau,\#\mathcal{C} and the corresponding degrees are computable. For compatible lists, the generators and every sublist ideal are computable over k1⁢(z)⁢[Θ±1]k_{1}(z)[\Theta^{\pm 1}]. Model (M-alg) requires no oracle, and (M-gen) uses (O1). For incompatible lists, the algorithm reports undetermined mixed constants and returns no ideal. Inputs supplied only by complex approximations are excluded. For values, the hypotheses of main-text Theorem 3 are required.

Proof.

The algorithm first rejects inadmissible specifications. It then closes and normalizes the list, retaining one representative per coordinate. It emits Xq−Xrep⁡(q)X_{q}-X_{\operatorname{rep}(q)} for every duplicate slot of every type. It emits Xc−cX_{c}-c for each listed constant c∈k1c\in k_{1}. Only distinct higher levels are free. Half-integer Bessel coordinates retain main-text Section 3’s exponential graphs. They also retain its derivative/order-shift graphs. The saturated lattice contains their rates ±c\pm c. They contribute no class to 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The algorithm preserves these graphs through closure and specialization. It also preserves them through saturation and contraction. It composes the linkage maps. Oracle (O1), followed by Hermite normal form, gives the minimal saturated lattice. Partial fractions and finite Taylor expansions determine the residues. Linear algebra then gives ρ\rho, κj⁢i\kappa_{ji} and the test for e(0,0)∈𝒱rese_{(0,0)}\in\mathcal{V}_{\rm res}; τ=∑η(hη−1)\tau=\sum_{\eta}(h_{\eta}-1) is the number of distinct retained levels (η,k)(\eta,k) with k≥2k\geq 2. (S2.3) cj={γj−∑iκj⁢i⁢γi,base-point,−lim0rj⁢(z,eλ1⁢z,…,eλd⁢z),origin.c_{j}=\begin{cases}\gamma_{j}-\sum_{i}\kappa_{ji}\gamma_{i},&\text{base-point}% ,\\ -\lim_{0}r_{j}(z,e^{\lambda_{1}z},\ldots,e^{\lambda_{d}z}),&\text{origin}.\end% {cases}

Any supplied normalization comparisons are applied before this step. Next adjoin inverse variables with relations Θh⁢Θh−1−1\Theta_{h}\Theta_{h}^{-1}-1, saturate, and eliminate. Appendix S3 Comparison of linear independence estimates

Main-text Theorem 4 has an explicit threshold H0H_{0}. It is too large for practical small-height tests. Galochkin’s measure [19, theorem, p. 241] applies to the algebraically independent pair (e−z,Ein⁡(z))(e^{-z},\operatorname{Ein}(z)). Multiplication of our form by e−1e^{-1} gives the polynomial of degree at most two b+a⁢x+c⁢x2+d⁢x⁢yb+ax+cx^{2}+dxy at (x,y)=(e−1,Ein⁡(1))(x,y)=(e^{-1},\operatorname{Ein}(1)). This gives a power-type bound with unevaluated constant. Bertrand–Beukers [8, Theorem 1, p. 182] give the multiplicity estimate for this four-function system; Bertrand–Chirskii–Yebbou [9, Theorem 1.2, p. 245] make its Shidlovskii constant effectively computable. These are inputs to effective measures. They give no numerical constants for this quadruple. Shidlovskii’s linear independence measure [36, Chapter 11, §2, Theorem 1, (32), p. 357] gives the following bound for the rational system (1,ez,e−z,Ein⁡(z))(1,e^{z},e^{-z},\operatorname{Ein}(z)) at the ordinary point 11: for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there is cε>0c_{\varepsilon}>0, depending only on ε\varepsilon and this fixed system and point, such that every (a,b,c,d)∈ℤ4∖{0}(a,b,c,d)\in\mathbb{Z}^{4}\setminus\{0\} satisfies |a+b⁢e+c⁢e−1+d⁢Ein⁡(1)|>cε⁢H−3−ε\lvert a+be+ce^{-1}+d\operatorname{Ein}(1)\rvert>c_{\varepsilon}H^{-3-\varepsilon}, where H=max⁡{|a|,|b|,|c|,|d|}≥1H=\max\{\lvert a\rvert,\lvert b\rvert,\lvert c\rvert,\lvert d\rvert\}\geq 1. Functional linear independence is required. The proof is on pp. 357–359. The book does not evaluate the positive constant. Fischler–Rivoal state the rational case as Theorem A. Their extension is Theorem 1 [18, pp. 2–3]. Page 3 discusses effectiveness in principle. It does not compute the constants. Their Theorem 1 assumes a nonzero linear form. For (a,b,c,d)∈ℤ4∖{0}(a,b,c,d)\in\mathbb{Z}^{4}\setminus\{0\}, Theorem 3 implies a+b⁢e+c⁢e−1+d⁢Ein⁡(1)≠0a+be+ce^{-1}+d\operatorname{Ein}(1)\neq 0. Main-text Theorem 4 evaluates the constants. Its exponent −60-60 is weaker. The threshold H0=NNH_{0}=N^{N} is astronomically large. The displayed bound applies for H≥H0H\geq H_{0}. Below H0H_{0}, scaling the coefficient vector gives only |Λ|≥H/(12⁢(2⁢H0)61)|\Lambda|\geq H/(12(2H_{0})^{61}). Main-text Appendix D evaluates the ν=μ=4\nu=\mu=4 polynomial-and-derivative construction of Adamczewski–Faverjon. A direct cyclic-vector Wronskian bound replaces a general zero estimate. This section records the comparison with Galochkin’s measure and the multiplicity estimates of Bertrand–Beukers and Bertrand–Chirskii–Yebbou. For classical background, Fel’dman–Nesterenko’s monograph [15] is a further reference. Beukers points to its Theorem 5.23 for the qualitative Siegel–Shidlovskii theorem [10, p. 369]. This comparison attributes no further exponent or evaluated constant to the monograph.

Appendix S5 Classical single-family results

For one scale, the resonant Bessel triple is classical. Mahler proved independence of values of J0,J0′J_{0},J^{\prime}_{0} and order derivatives of normalized JλJ_{\lambda} at λ=0\lambda=0 [29, Theorem 2, p. 167]. His Theorem 3, pp. 169–170, rewrites these values with connection constants. In particular, he proves that π⁢Y0⁢(2)/(2⁢J0⁢(2))−γ\pi Y_{0}(2)/(2J_{0}(2))-\gamma is transcendental [29, Theorem 3 and its consequence, pp. 169–170]. His KλK_{\lambda} denotes normalized ordinary Bessel JJ, not modified KK. Belogrivov treated each nonnegative integer order at nonzero algebraic points and the determinant relation z⁢(u1′⁢u0−u1⁢u0′)+u02=1z(u^{\prime}_{1}u_{0}-u_{1}u^{\prime}_{0})+u_{0}^{2}=1 [7, Theorem 4, Lemmas 4–5, (36)]. His coordinates are u0,λ⁢(ζ)=Kλ⁢(ζ)u_{0,\lambda}(\zeta)=K_{\lambda}(\zeta) and u1,λ⁢(ζ)=∂λKλ⁢(ζ)u_{1,\lambda}(\zeta)=\partial_{\lambda}K_{\lambda}(\zeta), with the same normalized ordinary Bessel convention. Thus u0,0⁢(i⁢c⁢z)=Ic⁢(z)u_{0,0}(icz)=I_{c}(z) and u1,0⁢(i⁢c⁢z)=−Sc⁢(z)u_{1,0}(icz)=-S_{c}(z). His primes are derivatives in ζ\zeta; substitution gives z⁢(Ic⁢Wc−Vc⁢Sc)−Ic2+1=0z(I_{c}W_{c}-V_{c}S_{c})-I_{c}^{2}+1=0. His Kummer-pair theorems treat values of F11⁢(μ;ν;z){}_{1}F_{1}(\mu;\nu;z) and its derivative at several points, without the logarithmic companion [6, Theorems 1–2]. The one-point corollary over the full ℰ\mathcal{E} is known from Shidlovskii’s simultaneous exponential-integral theorem [36, Chapter 7, §1, Theorem 1, pp. 232–233] by the finite-rate reduction below. Mahler’s final integral family was announced without proof [29, §23, pp. 172–173], as Rivoal notes [35, §7]. Put G0⁢(z)=∫0∞e−t⁢(t+z)−1⁢𝑑tG_{0}(z)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}(t+z)^{-1}\,dt for z∈ℂ∖(−∞,0]z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty,0], and use the principal branch of log⁡z\log z [35, p. 1 of the author manuscript]. Rivoal proves his Theorem 2(ii) for every algebraic z∉(−∞,0]z\notin(-\infty,0] [35, Theorem 2(ii), §§5 and 7]: trdegℚ⁡ℚ⁢(γ+log⁡z,ez,G0⁢(z))≥2\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathbb{Q}(\gamma+\log z,e^{z},G_{0}(z))\geq 2. At z=1z=1, G0⁢(1)=δ=e⁢E1⁢(1)G_{0}(1)=\delta=eE_{1}(1), so this gives trdegℚ⁡ℚ⁢(e,γ,δ)≥2\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathbb{Q}(e,\gamma,\delta)\geq 2. The full ℰ\mathcal{E}-base conclusion is attributed to Shidlovskii’s simultaneous theorem, without adding an all-rate quantifier to Rivoal’s statement. Main-text Theorem 5 systematically assembles multi-node mixed families over the selected regular-coordinate field BB. The source comparison for that scope remains partial.

Finite-rate reduction for the known one-point consequence

Shidlovskii defines ω0⁢(z)=ez\omega_{0}(z)=e^{z} and ωk⁢(z)=1+∑n≥1zn/(n!⁢nk)\omega_{k}(z)=1+\sum_{n\geq 1}z^{n}/(n!n^{k}) for k≥1k\geq 1. Thus ω1⁢(−x)=1−Ein⁡(x)\omega_{1}(-x)=1-\operatorname{Ein}(x). For each integer m≥1m\geq 1 and each finite set of algebraic nodes ξ1,…,ξr\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{r} linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, his theorem gives simultaneous algebraic independence of ωk⁢(ξi)\omega_{k}(\xi_{i}), 0≤k≤m0\leq k\leq m, 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r. The reduction below uses m=1m=1. Fix algebraic x≠0x\neq 0. A polynomial relation for Ein⁡(x)\operatorname{Ein}(x) over ℰ\mathcal{E} has finitely many coefficients, each algebraic over a field generated by finitely many eβje^{\beta_{j}} with algebraic βj\beta_{j}. Extend η1=−x\eta_{1}=-x to a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-basis η1,…,ηr\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{r} of the span of −x-x and these rates. Clearing rational denominators makes every eβje^{\beta_{j}} algebraic over K=ℚ¯⁢(eη1,…,eηr)K={\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(e^{\eta_{1}},\ldots,e^{\eta_{r}}). The theorem with m=1m=1 makes ω1⁢(−x)\omega_{1}(-x) transcendental over KK. It remains transcendental over any algebraic extension containing the finitely many coefficients, excluding the proposed relation. At x=1x=1, Ein⁡(1)=γ+E1⁢(1)\operatorname{Ein}(1)=\gamma+E_{1}(1) and e∈ℰ×e\in\mathcal{E}^{\times}, giving the equivalent alternatives with E1⁢(1)E_{1}(1) and δ=e⁢E1⁢(1)\delta=eE_{1}(1). This reduction retains −x-x as a basis member. It does not retain arbitrary merely distinct nodes in a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-basis or adjoin regular Bessel/Kummer pairs; the mixed conclusion over BB uses main-text Theorem 3.

Powers treats odd and even multisections of iterated exponential integrals. He proves independence over the field generated by their level-zero functions. At 11, he proves independence over the corresponding value field [34, p. 13]. Belogrivov also treated one-node shifted-denominator hypergeometric families and argument derivatives [5].

Homogeneous and integration antecedents

Ostrowski makes primitive dependence explicit for rational-exponential derivatives [33, pp. 315–316]; Kolchin gives the general differential-algebraic setting [27]. Beukers, Brownawell and Heckman’s 1988 paper [11] is an antecedent for the differential-Galois method. BBH’s homogeneous framework supplies its normality characterization [11, Theorem 2.2, p. 288]. Its common-power descent assumes irreducible Siegel-normal systems [11, Proposition 2.4, pp. 291–292]. Gorelov invokes these results in his homogeneous reduction [23, Lemma 13, p. 7]. He identifies BBH’s omitted Bessel–Kummer linkage [23, Example 1, p. 3; Lemma 14, p. 7]. The second BBH result cited there is Proposition 2.4, not Theorem 2.4. His criteria characterize independence of fundamental-matrix entries with exponentials and of the values F(i)⁢(α)F^{(i)}(\alpha) [23, Theorems 1–2, pp. 4–5]. Appendix C checks the hypotheses for the homogeneous rank-two inputs used here. BBH Theorem 2.2(iv) requires an extension by scalars of SL2\operatorname{SL}_{2}. This is the rank-two group condition supplied by main-text Lemma 4.6. It includes the homogeneous logarithmic solution J=S−I⁢LJ=S-IL or J=Σ−F⁢LJ=\Sigma-FL. No normality assertion applies to the enlarged extension with LL and the E-parts separately.

Gorelov’s inhomogeneous generalized hypergeometric equation has scalar forcing ∏j=1q(λj−1)\prod_{j=1}^{q}(\lambda_{j}-1) [20, p. 663]. His inhomogeneous hypergeometric criteria require homogeneous-group and parameter hypotheses [20, Theorems 1–3, pp. 664–665]. For q>lq>l, his function criteria work over homogeneous fundamental-matrix fields. They require a homogeneous group containing SLq\operatorname{SL}_{q} [20, Theorems 1–2, p. 664]. Dependence occurs when a denominator parameter belongs to ℕ\mathbb{N}; for a collection, equivalent parameter vectors at equal scales also cause dependence. His value theorem requires rational parameters, odd q≥3q\geq 3, irreducibility exclusions and nonzero algebraic arguments. It also imposes four explicit collision conditions [20, Theorem 3, pp. 664–665]. These hypotheses are not conditions for our normalized logarithmic E-parts. In our resonant encoding, λ=(1,1)\lambda=(1,1) makes that scalar forcing vanish. The E-parts instead have forcing 2⁢I′2I^{\prime} or 2⁢F′−s⁢F2F^{\prime}-sF. Their name alone does not identify the two inhomogeneous problems.

Gorelov’s primitive dependence criterion is a constant-linear-combination criterion [20, Lemma 6, p. 670]. His integration result adjoins primitives of zδ⁢eω⁢zz^{\delta}e^{\omega z} over the specified homogeneous fields [20, Lemma 7, pp. 670–672]. Here δ\delta is his integration exponent, distinct from the Gompertz constant above. The nonzero rates are distinct, δ∉ℤ≥0\delta\notin\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, and same-rate exponents do not differ by integers. Independence of his fundamental-matrix, exponential and power functions is assumed. The case δ=−1\delta=-1 includes first-level exponential integrals. Lemma 8 concerns integration involving homogeneous solution cofactors. These are integration antecedents. They do not state the full finite-pole residue algorithm or its affine normalization constants.

BBH already discusses successive exponential integrals as a Liouville extension [11, p. 281]. Its successive series are ∑n≥1zn/(nj⁢n!)\sum_{n\geq 1}z^{n}/(n^{j}n!) through finite depth. They arise from successive inhomogeneous first-order equations, outside Siegel normality. This anticipates tower integration, without giving the present multi-node tower ideal or its degree.

Gorelov’s normalized integral family

For λ∈ℂ∖ℤ<0\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{Z}_{<0}, write ϕλ⁢(z)=F11⁢(1;λ+1;z)=∑n≥0zn/(λ+1)n\phi_{\lambda}(z)={}_{1}F_{1}(1;\lambda+1;z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}z^{n}/(\lambda+1)_{n}, so ϕλ⁢(0)=1\phi_{\lambda}(0)=1 [24, p. 384]. Gorelov’s later paper treats the specific family Vλ,ν,α⁢(z)=ν⁢z−ν⁢eα⁢z⁢∫0ztν−1⁢e−α⁢t⁢ϕλ⁢(t)⁢𝑑tV_{\lambda,\nu,\alpha}(z)=\allowbreak\nu z^{-\nu}e^{\alpha z}\allowbreak\int_{% 0}^{z}t^{\nu-1}e^{-\alpha t}\phi_{\lambda}(t)\,dt [24, pp. 383–384]. Here α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C} and λ,ν∈ℂ∖ℤ<0\lambda,\nu\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{Z}_{<0}. Explicitly, if e−α⁢z⁢ϕλ⁢(z)=∑n≥0an⁢zne^{-\alpha z}\phi_{\lambda}(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}a_{n}z^{n}, then Vλ,ν,α⁢(z)=eα⁢z⁢(a0+∑n≥1ν⁢an⁢zn/(ν+n))V_{\lambda,\nu,\alpha}(z)=e^{\alpha z}\bigl{(}a_{0}+\sum_{n\geq 1}\nu a_{n}z^{% n}/(\nu+n)\bigr{)}. This is Shidlovskii’s normalized primitive for ν∉ℤ<0\nu\notin\mathbb{Z}_{<0} [24, p. 384]; in particular, Vλ,0,α=eα⁢zV_{\lambda,0,\alpha}=e^{\alpha z}. The integral need not converge at zero for every allowed complex parameter. This family has Vλ,ν,α⁢(0)=1V_{\lambda,\nu,\alpha}(0)=1. It satisfies a second-order inhomogeneous equation and V′=(α−ν/z)⁢V+(ν/z)⁢ϕλV^{\prime}=(\alpha-\nu/z)V+(\nu/z)\phi_{\lambda} [24, p. 384; (17), p. 385]. Theorem 1 classifies its Laurent-polynomial representations in exponentials and ϕ\phi functions for the stated complex parameters. For members of this family that are E-functions, Theorem 2 classifies algebraic dependence of VV and V′V^{\prime} over ℂ⁢(z)\mathbb{C}(z) [24, pp. 384–385]. Lemma 3 gives a second-order inhomogeneous characterization of E-functions [24, p. 386]. Its value discussion concerns that family [24, Conclusion 1, p. 390]. Collections Vλ,ν,α⁢(ξ⁢z)V_{\lambda,\nu,\alpha}(\xi z) with varying parameters and scales are explicitly deferred [24, §4, item 2 (Conclusion 2), p. 390].

These works supply homogeneous, integration and value antecedents. They do not state the joint multi-scale normalized ideal with shared logarithmic E-parts, finite-pole residue relations, higher Ein towers and fixed additive constants. They also do not give the present actual connection-constant cancellation algebra. No global novelty conclusion follows from this comparison.

Earlier value inputs

Earlier value theorems have narrower inputs. BBH treats rational admissible homogeneous hypergeometric families [11, Corollary 4.6, pp. 300–301]. Gorelov imposes rational-parameter and collision conditions [20, Theorem 3, pp. 664–665]. His later result concerns one integral family, with Theorem 2 restricted to E-functions [24, Theorem 2, p. 385; Conclusion 1, p. 390]. These statements do not supply the present specialized normalized ideal.

Appendix S6 Examples and limits of coefficient cancellation

The first two examples illustrate the general algebraic distinction. For example, over algebraically closed BB, take a transcendental xx and X=xX=x, d=x/2d=x/2. Then V=x/2V=x/2 and B⁢[V]∩B⁢[X]=B⁢[x]B[V]\cap B[X]=B[x], although 𝒜d=B\mathcal{A}_{d}=B. If instead d=2⁢xd=2x, then P⁢(Z)=Z2P(Z)=Z^{2} gives P⁢(V)=P⁢(X)P(V)=P(X) without being translation invariant. Thus independence of XX over BB leaves mixed relations between XX and 𝐜\mathbf{c} undetermined, including the arithmetic nature of γ\gamma.

For connection values, use main-text Theorem 5’s notation. Linked entries must first be reduced. Contiguity and the determinant give

Γ⁢(a+1)⁢U⁢(a+1,1,t)fa+1⁢(t)−Γ⁢(a)⁢U⁢(a,1,t)fa⁢(t)=−eta⁢fa⁢(t)⁢fa+1⁢(t)∈B,\frac{\Gamma(a+1)U(a+1,1,t)}{f_{a+1}(t)}-\frac{\Gamma(a)U(a,1,t)}{f_{a}(t)}=-% \frac{e^{t}}{af_{a}(t)f_{a+1}(t)}\in B,

and the half-Kummer entry at (2⁢u,1/2)(2u,1/2) equals K0⁢(u)/I0⁢(u)K_{0}(u)/I_{0}(u). Higher Ein levels are excluded: their natural tail already satisfies ∫x∞e−v⁢log⁡(v/x)⁢𝑑v/v=12⁢(log⁡x+γ)2+π2/12−Ein2⁡(x)\int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-v}\log(v/x)\,dv/v=\tfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\gamma)^{2}+\pi^{2}% /12-\operatorname{Ein}_{2}(x). No reduction of this connection to B+B⁢γB+B\gamma is assumed.

Fischler–Rivoal’s Gamma-polynomial connection mechanism [16, Theorem 2(iii) and the subsequent discussion on p. 35] gives asymptotic coefficients at infinity. They have the form Γ⁢(α∗)⁢P⁢(γ)\Gamma(\alpha^{*})P(\gamma) over their ring of GG-values. Here α∗=1\alpha^{*}=1 for nonpositive integral α\alpha. Gauss’s digamma formula and recurrence are classical. Bundschuh [13, Corollary 1] proved transcendence of ψ⁢(a)+γ\psi(a)+\gamma for rational nonintegral aa. See also Murty–Saradha [31, Theorems 1, 3–4]. These results do not imply independence over the present BB.

Detailed coefficient-cancellation argument

Main-text Proposition 7.3 is an algebraic statement about the actual column dd, independent of its special-function origin. Write d=d0+M⁢ξd=d_{0}+M\xi with d0∈BNd_{0}\in B^{N}, rankB⁡M=κ\operatorname{rank}_{B}M=\kappa and 1,ξ1,…,ξκ1,\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{\kappa} independent over BB. For P∈𝒜dP\in\mathcal{A}_{d} of degree mm, let PjP_{j} be its homogeneous part of degree jj. The degree m−1m-1 part of P⁢(Z−d)P(Z-d) is

Pm−1⁢(Z)−d0⋅∇Pm⁢(Z)−∑jξj⁢Mj⋅∇Pm⁢(Z).P_{m-1}(Z)-d_{0}\cdot\nabla P_{m}(Z)-\sum_{j}\xi_{j}M_{j}\cdot\nabla P_{m}(Z).

Its coefficients lie in BB, so each Mj⋅∇Pm=0M_{j}\cdot\nabla P_{m}=0. Thus PmP_{m} is invariant under translation by im⁡M\operatorname{im}M and Pm⁢(Z−d)=Pm⁢(Z−d0)∈B⁢[Z]P_{m}(Z-d)=P_{m}(Z-d_{0})\in B[Z]. Subtract PmP_{m} and induct on degree. Conversely, this invariance makes P⁢(Z−d)=P⁢(Z−d0)∈B⁢[Z]P(Z-d)=P(Z-d_{0})\in B[Z]. Coordinates adapted to im⁡M\operatorname{im}M therefore give 𝒜d=B⁢[J⁢Z]\mathcal{A}_{d}=B[JZ]. Exact invariance additionally requires invariance under d0d_{0}. Iteration at integer multiples, followed by polynomial dependence on the translation parameter, gives invariance under B⁢d0Bd_{0}. The joint invariant algebra is B⁢[J0⁢Z]B[J_{0}Z].

Since J⁢d∈BN−κJd\in B^{N-\kappa}, B⁢[J⁢V]=B⁢[J⁢X]B[JV]=B[JX] and its transcendence degree is N−κN-\kappa. Since d=A⁢𝐜d=A\mathbf{c} and AA is algebraic, κ≤rankB⁡A=rankℚ¯⁡A\kappa\leq\operatorname{rank}_{B}A=\operatorname{rank}_{{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}% }}A. If the rows of a matrix QQ lie in row⁡(J)\operatorname{row}(J), then Q⁢d∈BsQd\in B^{s} and trdegB⁡B⁢(Q⁢V)=rankB⁡Q\operatorname{trdeg}_{B}B(QV)=\operatorname{rank}_{B}Q. Its relation ideal is generated by the linear row dependencies μ⁢W\mu W, μ⁢Q=0\mu Q=0: translation by Q⁢dQd preserves these equations because μ⁢Q⁢d=0\mu Qd=0. In particular J0⁢V=J0⁢XJ_{0}V=J_{0}X and trdegB⁡B⁢(J0⁢V)=rankB⁡J0\operatorname{trdeg}_{B}B(J_{0}V)=\operatorname{rank}_{B}J_{0}. The actual rank κ\kappa and matrix JJ are not claimed effective. For JAJ_{A} whose rows span the left kernel {λ∈B1×N:λ⁢A=0}\{\lambda\in B^{1\times N}:\lambda A=0\}, the uniform translation-invariant polynomial and rational algebras are B⁢[JA⁢Z]B[J_{A}Z] and B⁢(JA⁢Z)B(J_{A}Z). The actual row space {λ∈B1×N:λ⁢d∈B}\{\lambda\in B^{1\times N}:\lambda d\in B\}, spanned by the rows of JJ, contains the left kernel of AA and may give the larger coefficient-cancellation algebra 𝒜d=B⁢[J⁢Z]\mathcal{A}_{d}=B[JZ]. Once this row space is fixed, nonlinear relations among the entries of dd do not enlarge 𝒜d\mathcal{A}_{d}. Exact translation invariants are B⁢[J0⁢Z]B[J_{0}Z].

Computation for the mixed example

In main-text Example 7.2, choose x=1x=1, (u,m)=(2,0)(u,m)=(2,0) and (t,a)=(1,1/2)(t,a)=(1,1/2). Gauss’s formula gives G1/2=−2⁢log⁡2G_{1/2}=-2\log 2; its cotangent term vanishes and its sine sum is empty. All node logarithms and both recurrence corrections vanish. Thus

𝐜=(γlog⁡2),A=(10101−2),X=(Ein⁡(1),𝖲⁢(2)I0⁢(2),S1/2⁢(1)f1/2⁢(1))t,V=X−A⁢𝐜.\begin{gathered}\mathbf{c}=\binom{\gamma}{\log 2},\quad A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 1&0\\ 1&-2\end{pmatrix},\\ X=\left(\operatorname{Ein}(1),\frac{\mathsf{S}(2)}{I_{0}(2)},\frac{S_{1/2}(1)}% {f_{1/2}(1)}\right)^{t},\quad V=X-A\mathbf{c}.\end{gathered}

No additive π\pi entry is needed, despite the multiplicative Γ⁢(1/2)\Gamma(1/2) in the third connection value. The first two constants cancel:

E1⁢(1)−K0⁢(2)I0⁢(2)=Ein⁡(1)−𝖲⁢(2)I0⁢(2)=X1−X2.E_{1}(1)-\frac{K_{0}(2)}{I_{0}(2)}=\operatorname{Ein}(1)-\frac{\mathsf{S}(2)}{% I_{0}(2)}=X_{1}-X_{2}.

Main-text Theorem 5, via Theorem 3, gives independence of X1,X2X_{1},X_{2} over B∗B_{*}. Thus this difference is transcendental over B∗B_{*}, hence over ℰ\mathcal{E}, since a polynomial relation would contradict that independence.

What the actual-number bound asserts

Main-text Theorem 5 gives trdegF⁡F⁢(𝐜,V)≥N\operatorname{trdeg}_{F}F(\mathbf{c},V)\geq N for F=ℰ,BF=\mathcal{E},B. It assumes neither independence of 𝐜\mathbf{c} nor independence of XX over F⁢(𝐜)F(\mathbf{c}). For example, over an algebraically closed field FF, take independent X1,…,XNX_{1},\ldots,X_{N}, 𝐜=(X1)\mathbf{c}=(X_{1}) and d=(X1,0,…,0)d=(X_{1},0,\ldots,0). Then V=(0,X2,…,XN)V=(0,X_{2},\ldots,X_{N}) and the combined degree is NN, although 𝐜\mathbf{c} is transcendental. Thus the argument does not give the additive bound N+trdegF⁡F⁢(𝐜)N+\operatorname{trdeg}_{F}F(\mathbf{c}). The mixed example is a simultaneous consequence of the joint value theorem. Separate one-family statements alone do not yield independence after all regular pairs have been adjoined. No priority claim is made.
